Mitochondrial dysfunction and metabolic.research_question: In fibrotic tissue models, does localized, time-limited MMP activation combined with reversible complex I attenuation increase ECM turnover, restore intercellular connectivity, reduce cellular protein carbonylation, and improve organ function versus either intervention alone?
Mitochondrial dysfunction and metabolic.rationale: Short pulses of inflammation-associated proteases can clear extracellular protein garbage and help reestablish parabiosis, while glycolysis reduces ROS burden. Coordinating ECM clearance with a temporary ROS-sparing metabolic state should minimize intracellular re-oxidation and promote durable reconnection without the infectious risks of systemic anti-inflammatory therapy.

Mitochondrial dysfunction and metabolic.hypothesis: Oxidative carbonylation of mismatch repair and translational fidelity factors forms a feed-forward loop that destabilizes mitochondrial DNA maintenance proteins, increasing heteroplasmy and driving a ROS-sparing glycolytic reprogramming; targeted mitochondrial enrichment of chaperones and DJ-1 deglycase disrupts this loop.
Mitochondrial dysfunction and metabolic.research_question: Under oxidative stress, does selective carbonylation of MRS and ribosomal fidelity components impair mitochondrial DNA repair proteins, increase mtDNA heteroplasmy, and bias metabolism toward glycolysis, and can mitochondrial targeting of chaperones or DJ-1 prevent these changes?
Mitochondrial dysfunction and metabolic.rationale: Stress downregulates MRS and increases genetic variability; misfolding and mistranslation predispose proteins to oxidation, and oxidized proteomes compromise DNA repair. A carbonylation-driven impairment of fidelity and repair would preferentially damage mtDNA maintenance, shifting cells toward glycolysis; mitochondrial chaperone/DJ-1 activity should break the cycle.

Mitochondrial dysfunction and metabolic.hypothesis: Installing a synthetic glyoxylate bypass in mammalian mitochondria (mitochondria-targeted isocitrate lyase and malate synthase) will lower mitochondrial NADH generation, reduce electron pressure on the ETC, and thereby decrease mitochondrial ROS production to prevent NLRP3 inflammasome activation and reverse Warburg-like metabolic reprogramming during hyperinflammatory states such as COVID-19.
Mitochondrial dysfunction and metabolic.research_question: Does mitochondrial expression of bacterial isocitrate lyase and malate synthase in infected or LPS-stimulated immune cells reduce mitochondrial ROS, NLRP3 activation, and lactate accumulation while restoring ΔΨm and OXPHOS efficiency?
Mitochondrial dysfunction and metabolic.rationale: D. radiodurans suppresses endogenous ROS by inducing the glyoxylate bypass to limit NADH/FADH2 release. In COVID-19 and inflammatory states, mitochondrial dysfunction, elevated lactate, and oxidative stress drive NLRP3 activation. A mitochondrial glyoxylate shunt could mechanistically offload NADH production, lowering ETC-derived ROS and dampening inflammasome signaling while alleviating glycolytic reliance.

Mitochondrial dysfunction and metabolic.hypothesis: Targeting methylene blue to KRAS plasma-membrane nanoclusters to generate localized ROS (via MB’s redox cycling with NADH/O2) will selectively carbonylate KRAS at K42/R149, disrupting KRAS–RAF binding and downstream ERK signaling in glycolytic, redox-dysregulated tumors.
Mitochondrial dysfunction and metabolic.research_question: Do membrane-anchored methylene blue constructs that accumulate in KRAS nanoclusters induce site-specific KRAS carbonylation, reduce KRAS–RAF PPI and ERK phosphorylation, and inhibit tumor growth with minimal systemic oxidative damage?
Mitochondrial dysfunction and metabolic.rationale: Oxidative modifications at KRAS residues K42 and R149 disrupt KRAS–RBD interactions and signaling. Methylene blue can act as an electron shuttle from NADH to O2, locally producing ROS. Tumors exhibit ROS handling defects and elevated carbonylation; concentrating ROS generation at KRAS nanoclusters should mechanistically abrogate MAPK signaling while limiting off-target oxidation.

Mitochondrial dysfunction and metabolic.hypothesis: Engineering mitochondria-tethered, phase-separated condensates enriched in Mn2+, orthophosphate, PQQ, and cellular metabolites will act as artificial cytosolic redox-buffers that quench mitochondrial-origin ROS at the organelle surface, thereby preventing cytosolic protein carbonylation and NLRP3 activation during acute inflammation and viral infection.
Mitochondrial dysfunction and metabolic.research_question: Can outer-mitochondrial membrane–tethered Mn–PQQ–metabolite condensates reduce protein carbonyls and 8-oxoguanine in the cytosol and suppress NLRP3 activation in macrophages exposed to LPS or SARS-CoV-2 mimetics, without increasing intramitochondrial H2O2?
Mitochondrial dysfunction and metabolic.rationale: D. radiodurans protects its proteome via cytosolic Mn–metabolite complexes that rapidly scavenge ROS; however, in eukaryotic cells, Mn-driven redox inside mitochondria produces H2O2. Relocating Mn–metabolite chemistry to the mitochondrial surface and incorporating PQQ, a potent ROS detoxifier, could intercept ROS before it damages cytosolic proteins or triggers inflammasomes.

Mitochondrial dysfunction and metabolic.hypothesis: Pharmacologic or genetic enhancement of translational fidelity during inflammation reduces the pool of misfolded, oxidation-prone proteins, thereby decreasing carbonylation of ROS-handling enzymes (e.g., peroxiredoxins, thioredoxin, SOD), restoring ETC function and ΔΨm, and mitigating cytokine storm and fatigue phenotypes in COVID-19.
Mitochondrial dysfunction and metabolic.research_question: Do agents that increase ribosomal proofreading lower protein carbonylation, preserve PRDX/TXN/SOD integrity, improve mitochondrial membrane potential, and reduce lactate and cytokine levels in SARS-CoV-2–infected leukocytes?
Mitochondrial dysfunction and metabolic.rationale: Translation errors increase protein carbonylation at constant ROS and oxidative protein damage underlies morbidity. In COVID-19, oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and lactate accumulation are prominent. Protecting key antioxidant and ETC proteins by reducing mistranslation should mechanistically stabilize redox homeostasis and cellular energy output.

Mutation-rate plasticity and mutator dyn.hypothesis: Competence-mediated exposure to divergent extracellular DNA serves as a community-level mutator switch by titrating MutL and transiently disabling mismatch repair, thereby synchronizing SOS-driven diversification and horizontal gene transfer; subsequent restoration of MMR erects sequence-divergence–dependent barriers that precipitate rapid speciation.
Mutation-rate plasticity and mutator dyn.research_question: Does uptake or exposure to mismatched exogenous DNA quantitatively titrate MutL in competent bacteria to raise mutation and recombination rates during stress, and does the later restoration of MMR reduce interstrain recombination, creating a measurable ‘speciation burst’?
Mutation-rate plasticity and mutator dyn.rationale: MMR efficiency decreases when mismatch repair proteins are titrated by high concentrations of mismatched DNA, and MutL is the limiting factor. Stress induces SOS, alleviates restriction barriers, and increases HGT, while accumulated polymorphism plus restored MMR suppresses recombination across sequence divergence. Thus, extracellular heterologous DNA can function as an ‘evo-signal’ that transiently elevates mutation and recombination at the community level and then enforces genetic isolation.

Mutation-rate plasticity and mutator dyn.hypothesis: A cAMP–CRP-controlled translational attenuator in mutL provides a metabolic gate for mutation-rate plasticity: carbon starvation raises cAMP, downregulates MutL protein independently of full SOS induction, creating a MutL-limited, low-SOS mutator state that accelerates adaptation while minimizing lesion-bypass mutagenesis.
Mutation-rate plasticity and mutator dyn.research_question: Does carbon starvation/cAMP signaling reduce MutL protein via CRP-dependent transcriptional or translational control and produce a mutator phenotype (increased mutation rate and MutL foci scarcity) without global SOS activation?
Mutation-rate plasticity and mutator dyn.rationale: Metabolic cAMP signaling has been shown to trigger genetic change. Because MutL is the limiting component that determines MMR saturation and MutL foci frequency tracks mutation rate, a CRP-responsive regulatory element in mutL could provide a rapid, energetically efficient mutator switch during starvation, complementing or preceding full SOS induction.

Mutation-rate plasticity and mutator dyn.hypothesis: Stressed bacterial subpopulations trigger undirected mismatch repair on unmethylated heteroduplex DNA to self-induce lethal double-strand breaks, releasing mismatch-rich DNA fragments that act as an altruistic ‘mutagenic necrosignal’ to saturate MMR and induce SOS/HGT in surviving neighbors, accelerating community adaptation.
Mutation-rate plasticity and mutator dyn.research_question: In biofilms under genotoxic or nutritional stress, are extracellular DNA fragments enriched for mismatches, and does their addition experimentally increase MutL titration, SOS markers, mutation/HGT rates, and overall survival of the remaining population?
Mutation-rate plasticity and mutator dyn.rationale: Undirected MMR can be lethal by causing double-strand breaks. Mutators can serve as genetic altruists at the population level. SOS induces replication of mobile elements and restriction alleviation, enhancing gene flow, while mismatched DNA can titrate MMR. Together this suggests a programmed death–mediated release of mismatch-rich DNA that drives a mutator transition and HGT in survivors.

Mutation-rate plasticity and mutator dyn.hypothesis: Noisy partitioning of MutL during cell division creates transiently heritable, low-MMR ‘scout’ lineages that exhibit elevated mutation and homeologous recombination for several generations before re-equilibrating, implementing a bet-hedging strategy that enables rapid adaptation without fixing mutator alleles.
Mutation-rate plasticity and mutator dyn.research_question: Do single-cell lineages tracked over multiple generations show stable-to-transient MutL scarcity (low foci, lower copy number) with concomitant increases in mutation and recombination rates that revert without changes in mutL genotype or sustained SOS activation?
Mutation-rate plasticity and mutator dyn.rationale: MutL foci intensities vary widely across cells and correlate with mutation frequency, implying variable functional MMR capacity. Given the divergent selection on mutation rates—high during adaptation, low afterward—stochastic, multi-generation MutL depletion through protein partitioning noise could realize a mechanistic bet-hedging strategy without genetic mutator fixation.

Mutation-rate plasticity and mutator dyn.hypothesis: The SOS-triggered cI→cro epigenetic switch co-installs a heritable, lineage-specific mutator state by transiently attenuating methyl-directed mismatch repair (MutHLS/Dam), thereby raising mutation rates in cro-dominant lineages while avoiding lethal undirected repair.
Mutation-rate plasticity and mutator dyn.research_question: Does switching to the cro-dominant state during SOS activation reduce Dam/MutHLS activity and elevate mutation rates specifically in those lineages relative to non-switched siblings under the same genotoxic stress?
Mutation-rate plasticity and mutator dyn.rationale: Genotoxic agents (UV, MNNG) simultaneously elevate epigenetic switching and mutational events, and the mutagenic effect is under the same epigenetic (SOS) control as prophage induction. Undirected mismatch repair is lethal but its lethality can be alleviated by mutHLS defects, suggesting that coordinating SOS-driven switching with partial MMR suppression could safely generate a mutator subpopulation. The mutual repression of cI/cro provides heritable memory for both the transcriptional state and an associated repair mode.

Mutation-rate plasticity and mutator dyn.hypothesis: Strand-discrimination noise in mismatch repair acts as an active driver of the cI→cro epigenetic decision by generating operator-proximal excision tracts and single-strand gaps that destabilize cI binding and bias Cro occupancy; fully undirected repair triggers lethal processing that eliminates non-switched cells, enriching for cro-on lineages.
Mutation-rate plasticity and mutator dyn.research_question: Does transient weakening of strand-discrimination signals (e.g., partial Dam inhibition) increase cI→cro switching probability via detectable operator-proximal MMR excision footprints, and does complete loss of directionality selectively kill non-switched cells?
Mutation-rate plasticity and mutator dyn.rationale: SOS induction flips the switch by RecA-mediated cI cleavage, yet UV/MNNG produce a predominance of epigenetic switches over stable mutants, implying an upstream DNA processing bias. Because undirected MMR is lethal and its lethality is mitigated by mutHLS defects, fluctuations in MMR directionality near the operator could both bias the switch and cull cells that fail to switch.

Mutation-rate plasticity and mutator dyn.hypothesis: The cro-dominant state functions as an epigenetic-to-genetic ratchet by locally elevating mutation rates at the cI locus through transcription-coupled error-prone repair, converting transient SOS-induced switching into permanent cI loss-of-function in a subset of lineages.
Mutation-rate plasticity and mutator dyn.research_question: Do cro-on cells exhibit a higher, locus-specific mutation rate at cI (relative to housekeeping loci) that depends on SOS polymerases and dampened mismatch repair, thereby fixing the switched (gal+) state genetically?
Mutation-rate plasticity and mutator dyn.rationale: A cI-inactivating mutation makes gal+ constitutive in all descendants, and mutational gal+ colonies are rare spontaneously but epigenetic switching dominates after UV. Because mutagenesis is under SOS control, a cro-on transcriptional burst through the cI region combined with error-prone repair could target and lock in the switched state.

Mutation-rate plasticity and mutator dyn.hypothesis: A bet-hedging circuit couples epigenetic switching to selective lethality via undirected mismatch repair: after DNA damage, cells that fail to flip to cro-on preferentially die from undirected MMR processing, while cro-on cells survive because SOS concurrently attenuates MutHLS, shifting the population toward a high-mutation-rate cro-on subpopulation.
Mutation-rate plasticity and mutator dyn.research_question: Under controlled genotoxic stress, do cI-on cells die more frequently from MMR-dependent lethality than cro-on cells, and is this selective filter abolished in mutHLS-deficient backgrounds?
Mutation-rate plasticity and mutator dyn.rationale: Undirected mismatch repair is lethal but its lethality can be relieved by mutHLS mutations; the mutagenic effect of damaging agents is under the same epigenetic (SOS) control as prophage induction, and damage produces a strong epigenetic switching response. These observations suggest a coordinated program where switching protects from MMR lethality and simultaneously elevates mutability in survivors.

Mutation-rate plasticity and mutator dyn.hypothesis: Oxidative stress triggers SOS-regulated, targeted proteolysis of MutS/MutL via Lon/ClpXP-like proteases, acting as a redox-sensitive mutator switch that drives MAC; stabilizing MutS/MutL (e.g., degron mutation or protease inhibition) will specifically suppress stress-induced mutagenesis without impairing basal fidelity.
Mutation-rate plasticity and mutator dyn.research_question: Does ROS exposure induce post-translational modifications that expose degrons on MutS/MutL, leading to their SOS-driven proteolysis and transient MMR downregulation, and can blocking this proteolysis selectively abolish MAC in aging colonies and during host colonization?
Mutation-rate plasticity and mutator dyn.rationale: MAC depends on oxidative metabolism and SOS, and is suppressed by MutS overproduction, suggesting MMR downregulation is causal. Protease inhibitors suppress multiple SOS outcomes, implying a proteolytic hub; we propose MutS/MutL are direct proteolytic targets under oxidative stress, creating a reversible mutator state.

Mutation-rate plasticity and mutator dyn.hypothesis: Biofilm oxygen and nutrient gradients create spatially segregated mutator microdomains at the oxic periphery via SOS/cAMP-dependent MAC, which generate adaptive mutations that are exported into interior MMR+ cells through SOS-stimulated recombination—forming a ‘mutation pump’ that accelerates adaptation while containing mutator costs.
Mutation-rate plasticity and mutator dyn.research_question: In microfluidic biofilms with controlled O2 gradients, do edge cells exhibit elevated mutation rates and SOS activity that generate beneficial alleles, which subsequently recombine into core MMR+ cells, and does flattening the gradient or blocking cAMP/SOS collapse this mutation–recombination flux?
Mutation-rate plasticity and mutator dyn.rationale: Structured environments and gradients are known; MAC requires SOS and cAMP and is reduced anaerobically, implying edge-localized mutagenesis in oxic zones. SOS stimulates recombination while MMR inhibits it, enabling transfer of adaptive variants away from mutators into stable backgrounds.

Mutation-rate plasticity and mutator dyn.hypothesis: Periodic loss and reacquisition of MMR (via stress-induced mutator phases followed by horizontal transfer of functional alleles) produces punctuated bursts of sequence divergence and, upon MMR restoration, immediate recombination barriers—constituting a rapid, cyclical route to bacterial speciation.
Mutation-rate plasticity and mutator dyn.research_question: Do experimental metapopulations forced through cycles of MMR loss and HGT-mediated restoration evolve recombination barriers faster than controls, and is the barrier strength predicted by the duration/intensity of the mutator phase and the mosaicism of reacquired MMR alleles?
Mutation-rate plasticity and mutator dyn.rationale: Mutator lines diverge rapidly and, once MMR is restored, recombination is inhibited by accrued divergence. MMR genes are repeatedly lost and reacquired via HGT and show mosaicism; SOS modulates recombination, suggesting an ecological cycle that can accelerate reproductive isolation.

Mutation-rate plasticity and mutator dyn.hypothesis: SOS-induced, VSP mismatch repair–mediated short-patch recombination preferentially transfers clustered adaptive SNP tracts from mutator genomes into MMR+ genomes during stress, accelerating the decoupling of beneficial alleles from mutator backgrounds and hastening mutator decline after adaptation.
Mutation-rate plasticity and mutator dyn.research_question: In mixed mutator/non-mutator populations adapting to stress, are new adaptive variants found as clustered short tracts in MMR+ recipients consistent with VSPMR patchwork recombination, and does disabling SOS or VSPMR reduce this transfer and prolong mutator linkage to adaptive alleles?
Mutation-rate plasticity and mutator dyn.rationale: Hypermutation produces adaptive alleles in mutators, while SOS stimulates recombination. VSPMR generates patchwork exchanges, and recombination can separate adaptive mutations from mutator alleles; this mechanism predicts a directional shunting of adaptive tracts into stable MMR+ genomes.

Mutation-rate plasticity and mutator dyn.hypothesis: A synthetic, starvation/oxidative-stress–responsive MutS toggle (e.g., ssrA-tagging of MutS under cAMP/ROS control) will provide a programmable transient mutator state that enhances early gut colonization when mutation supply is limiting, then restores MMR to preserve robustness and minimize long-term fitness costs.
Mutation-rate plasticity and mutator dyn.research_question: Do engineered probiotics bearing a degron-based MutS instability circuit under cAMP/ROS-inducible control show superior early colonization and adaptation in gnotobiotic mice, with restored low mutation rates and cross-environment fitness compared to constitutive mutators and wild type?
Mutation-rate plasticity and mutator dyn.rationale: Mutation supply limits early colonization and mutators enjoy a transient advantage but pay later costs; MAC is stress/ROS-driven and MutS dosage tunes MAC. A controlled MutS degradation–reexpression circuit should ‘gear-shift’ mutation-rate plasticity to capture benefits and avoid costs.

Mutation-rate plasticity and mutator dyn.hypothesis: Oxidative carbonylation of mismatch-repair proteins, especially MutS and MutL, acts as a stress-sensing switch that transiently down-tunes MMR to elevate both point mutation and recombination between diverged repeats; this switch is gated by growth-state-dependent MutS abundance and buffered by Mn(II)-mediated proteome protection.
Mutation-rate plasticity and mutator dyn.research_question: Does ROS-driven protein carbonylation target MutS/MutL for Lon/Clp-mediated proteolysis, thereby reducing MMR activity, increasing nascent mutation (MutL foci) and recombination between diverged repeats under stress, and can Mn(II) supplementation or carbonylation-resistant MutL/MutS mutants restore baseline mutation and recombination rates?
Mutation-rate plasticity and mutator dyn.rationale: Protein damage levels predict spontaneous mutation rates and multiple stress phenotypes, and MutS levels drop in nutrient-deprived/late stationary phase. Inactivation of MMR selectively increases recombination between diverged repeats, and MutL foci report nascent mutations. Thus, ROS-driven proteome damage could directly throttle MMR, coupling environmental redox state to mutation-rate plasticity, which is buffered by Mn(II)-protected proteomes.

Mutation-rate plasticity and mutator dyn.hypothesis: Interspecies conjugation triggers an SOS-dependent, recombination-specific mutator state via targeted downregulation of MutL, enhancing recombination with divergent DNA while leaving base-substitution fidelity largely intact.
Mutation-rate plasticity and mutator dyn.research_question: During interspecies mating, does SOS induction activate LexA-regulated effectors (e.g., proteases or sRNAs) that reduce MutL abundance/activity, thereby explaining the strong LexA dependence of interspecies recombination and the ability to increase introgression without elevating base-substitution mutagenesis?
Mutation-rate plasticity and mutator dyn.rationale: Mating induces a bona fide SOS response, and LexA-regulated functions are disproportionately required for interspecies versus intraspecies recombination. Partial reduction of MutL increases recombination between diverged sequences without a mutator phenotype, suggesting cells can naturally decouple recombination from point mutagenesis during HGT.

Mutation-rate plasticity and mutator dyn.hypothesis: Multicellular aggregation under genotoxic or nutrient stress establishes a 'community mutator' state in which localized SOS activation in dying subpopulations propagates via extracellular DNA and recombination to neighboring cells while nutrient deprivation lowers MutS levels, jointly elevating HGT, transposition, and recombination-driven adaptation.
Mutation-rate plasticity and mutator dyn.research_question: Do clumped/biofilm bacterial populations exhibit spatially correlated increases in SOS activity, HGT/transposition, and reduced MMR (via decreased MutS) that together accelerate adaptive evolution compared to dispersed cells, and can disrupting aggregation or SOS signaling suppress this collective mutator dynamic?
Mutation-rate plasticity and mutator dyn.rationale: Cell clumping increases survival under extreme stress and SOS induction boosts transformation, transduction, and transposition, while MutS levels drop in stationary phase. Aggregation could therefore coordinate a transient mutator window that leverages HGT and recombination as communal stress responses.

Mutation-rate plasticity and mutator dyn.hypothesis: A manganese redox rheostat in Deinococcus radiodurans controls mutation-rate plasticity by buffering proteome oxidation: optimal Mn(II)-mediated protection favors high-fidelity repair, whereas perturbed Mn redox cycling increases protein carbonylation, diminishes replication/repair fidelity, and biases genome reconstitution toward repeat-mediated amplifications and rearrangements.
Mutation-rate plasticity and mutator dyn.research_question: Do controlled perturbations of Mn(II)/ROS levels in D. radiodurans modulate protein carbonylation, MMR capacity, and the balance between precise double-strand break repair versus repeat-driven amplifications/rearrangements during post-IR genome reconstitution, and can engineering Mn-binding proteome components tune these outcomes?
Mutation-rate plasticity and mutator dyn.rationale: Excess Mn perturbs redox cycling and increases mutagenesis, while protein carbonylation strongly predicts mutation rate. D. radiodurans readily amplifies repeat-flanked regions, and extreme IR doses cause rearrangements likely from aberrant repair. A Mn-centric proteome protection mechanism could therefore set the repair/mutagenesis balance after massive DNA damage.

Mutation-rate plasticity and mutator dyn.hypothesis: IR-induced proteome carbonylation in parental rotifers/nematodes establishes a persistent, heritable reduction in mismatch repair capacity, creating a transgenerational mutator state that manifests as delayed reproductive death in descendants.
Mutation-rate plasticity and mutator dyn.research_question: After parental irradiation, do F1/F2 germlines exhibit reduced MMR protein abundance/activity and increased nascent mutation markers, and is this transgenerational mutator state preventable by parental antioxidant treatments that limit proteome carbonylation?
Mutation-rate plasticity and mutator dyn.rationale: Parental IR causes matched fecundity loss in progeny and correlates with proteome carbonylation, implying long-lived, self-propagating alterations. Given the potency of eukaryotic MMR, a heritable, oxidation-driven decrement in MMR offers a mechanistic route to delayed, dose-dependent reproductive failure across generations.

Mutation-rate plasticity and mutator dyn.hypothesis: Starvation-induced S-adenosylmethionine (SAM) depletion transiently inverts Dam/MMR dynamics to an 'error-fixing' regime analogous to dam mutants, selectively increasing transitions and frameshifts without full SOS activation as a low-cost mutator switch during nutrient scarcity.
Mutation-rate plasticity and mutator dyn.research_question: Does metabolic SAM limitation under carbon starvation recapitulate dam-like mutational spectra via altered MMR strand discrimination that favors error fixation, and can methionine/SAM supplementation suppress starvation-induced mutagenesis independently of the SOS pathway?
Mutation-rate plasticity and mutator dyn.rationale: Dam defects can convert MMR into an error-fixing mutator, and nutrient stress reduces MMR capacity while starvation can drive 'adaptive mutations.' A metabolic lever on methylation state provides a plausible, non-genetic mechanism to transiently elevate mutation rates with specific spectra under resource limitation.

Mutation-rate plasticity and mutator dyn.hypothesis: During conjugative transfer, the F plasmid transiently inhibits host mismatch repair (MMR) via an F-encoded, FinOP-regulated anti-MutS/MutL factor, locally elevating mutation rates and relaxing homology barriers around the transferred DNA to accelerate plasmid integration and adaptive diversification.
Mutation-rate plasticity and mutator dyn.research_question: Does the F plasmid express a peptide or sRNA during conjugation that binds or destabilizes MutS/MutL, thereby increasing local mutagenesis and intergenomic recombination near the T-DNA entry site?
Mutation-rate plasticity and mutator dyn.rationale: F shows a strong life-cycle dependence of mutation rate with marked elevation during conjugal transfer, while MMR sets homology-dependent barriers to recombination. Transient chemical or genetic inactivation of MMR greatly increases interspecies recombination and mutator enrichment. FinOP controls donor ability, suggesting F-encoded regulation could coordinate an anti-MMR activity during mating to enhance spread and fixation.

Mutation-rate plasticity and mutator dyn.hypothesis: The sigmaS stress regulon functions as an evolvability oscillator that coordinates bursts of mutagenesis by upregulating Pol IV and transposition (via hha) while post-translationally downregulating MMR activity through stress proteases or sequestration; the cAMP/oxidative-metabolism tuning of sigmaS sets the amplitude and timing of mutation bursts that drive stepwise diversification and subsequent speciation once MMR is restored.
Mutation-rate plasticity and mutator dyn.research_question: Does sigmaS activation trigger a measurable reduction in MutS/MutL activity or abundance during stationary phase and starvation, and do cyclic sigmaS dynamics produce temporally pulsed increases in mutation/transposition that correlate with selection strength and stress frequency?
Mutation-rate plasticity and mutator dyn.rationale: SigmaS stabilizes under diverse stresses and elevates Pol IV and transposition, and stress-induced mutagenesis scales with selection strength. MAC is controlled by sigmaS and cAMP, and natural isolates show large variability consistent with local tuning. A mechanism coupling sigmaS to transient MMR downregulation would parsimoniously explain strong but temporary mutagenesis pulses with low long-term cost and stepwise evolutionary jumps.

Mutation-rate plasticity and mutator dyn.hypothesis: Mismatch repair acts as a real-time sensor of sequence divergence that, when encountering high mismatch density in recombination intermediates, triggers an 'adaptive barrier' program via RecA/SOS signaling: switching on translesion polymerases and transposition while actively curtailing recombination with divergent DNA, thereby coupling mutagenesis bursts to the active establishment of species boundaries.
Mutation-rate plasticity and mutator dyn.research_question: Do engineered recombination events with graded mismatch loads activate SOS and mutagenesis in an MMR- and RecA-dependent manner, and does this response include nucleolytic termination of recombination with highly divergent DNA while permitting mutagenic repair?
Mutation-rate plasticity and mutator dyn.rationale: MMR and SOS jointly set recombination barriers that scale with sequence divergence, and MMR loss relaxes these barriers enabling interspecies mosaics. SOS increases genetic variability and recombination gene expression. A feedback from MMR mismatch sensing to SOS would mechanistically link perceived divergence to a concerted increase in mutagenesis and enforcement of reproductive isolation.

Mutation-rate plasticity and mutator dyn.hypothesis: Conjugation micro-niches in biofilms act as localized evolvability hotspots: FinOP-mediated amplifier cell interactions massively increase ssDNA flux during transfer, inducing SOS in donors and recipients; combined with sigmaS-driven stress programs, this creates spatially confined hypermutation and transposition near integration sites that seed genomic islands and multi-resistance clusters.
Mutation-rate plasticity and mutator dyn.research_question: In biofilms containing amplifier cells, are mutation and transposition rates elevated specifically around conjugation contact zones and plasmid integration loci in an SOS- and sigmaS-dependent fashion?
Mutation-rate plasticity and mutator dyn.rationale: Amplifier cells and FinOP interactions can elevate transfer rates by orders of magnitude. Conjugation exposes ssDNA and triggers stress, conditions that induce SOS polymerases and boost genetic variability; sigmaS also promotes transposition. Co-localization of these processes in biofilms predicts spatially patterned hypermutation and mobile element activity at HGT interfaces.

Mutation-rate plasticity and mutator dyn.hypothesis: Anti-evolvability therapy can purge mutator lineages and block horizontal gene flow in chronic infections by combining a mutationally hard-to-escape bactericidal pulse (e.g., high-dose ampicillin) with transient elevation of MMR activity (e.g., phage-delivered MutL overexpression) to both suppress mutation supply and re-tighten recombination barriers.
Mutation-rate plasticity and mutator dyn.research_question: Does sequential therapy with high-dose ampicillin followed by bacteriophage-mediated MutL overexpression reduce mutator frequency and HGT-driven resistance acquisition in vivo compared to standard regimens?
Mutation-rate plasticity and mutator dyn.rationale: Failed therapies select mutators that undermine subsequent treatments; high-dose ampicillin alone can eliminate mutators when single-step resistance is unlikely. Overexpressed MutL abolishes induced hyperrecombination and, together with intact MMR, enforces recombination barriers. Coordinating these could collapse mutator subpopulations and impede resistance spread.

Mutation-rate plasticity and mutator dyn.hypothesis: Proteome damage-driven chaperone sequestration establishes a threshold-controlled mutator switch by transiently uncoupling MutS/MutL from the replisome and lowering replicative fidelity.
Mutation-rate plasticity and mutator dyn.research_question: Does increasing cytosolic misfolded-protein load (without added DNA damage) redistribute DnaK/Tig/GroEL away from replication forks, reduce MutS/MutL engagement at nascent mismatches, and produce a sharp, reversible increase in genome-wide mutation rate once a proteome-carbonylation threshold is crossed?
Mutation-rate plasticity and mutator dyn.rationale: Oxidative proteome damage (PC) tightly tracks spontaneous and induced mutation rates, and chaperone availability strongly modulates mutagenesis. We hypothesize that misfolded proteins titrate core chaperones away from fidelity factors (replicative proofreading and MMR assembly), functionally saturating MMR and lowering replication fidelity until proteostasis is restored.

Mutation-rate plasticity and mutator dyn.hypothesis: Intracellular Mn2+/Fe balance acts as a rheostat for evolvability by tuning proteome oxidation; optimizing Mn2+ availability suppresses mutator states, while Mn2+ depletion and iron release from damaged Fe–S enzymes trigger transient mutator episodes.
Mutation-rate plasticity and mutator dyn.research_question: Can controlled modulation of Mn2+ (and Fe) levels lower proteome carbonylation and mutation rates in mutator-prone cells (e.g., mutH−, low-fidelity ribosome strains) and, conversely, can transient Mn2+ withdrawal combined with iron overload induce a reversible, PC-mediated mutator state without directly perturbing DNA repair genes?
Mutation-rate plasticity and mutator dyn.rationale: Mn2+ homeostasis shapes oxidative stress, while Fe–S enzyme damage releases iron that amplifies ROS. Because proteome oxidation, not DNA lesion load per se, sets mutation rates, metal-ion tuning should provide a metabolic handle to switch evolvability on/off.

Mutation-rate plasticity and mutator dyn.hypothesis: A proteostasis–genome fidelity feedback loop creates a bistable ‘error catastrophe’ switch: elevated translational errors misfold replication/repair proteins (e.g., DnaQ, MutL), saturate MMR, and escalate Pol III misincorporation, while high ribosomal fidelity or chaperone overexpression pushes the system back to a low-mutation basin.
Mutation-rate plasticity and mutator dyn.research_question: Does increasing translational error rate alone (via ribosomal fidelity mutations) drive cells across a measurable proteome-damage threshold into a high-mutation state characterized by reduced DnaQ proofreading and diminished MMR capacity, and is this bistability reversible by boosting chaperone capacity or restoring ribosomal accuracy?
Mutation-rate plasticity and mutator dyn.rationale: Low translational fidelity increases mutation frequencies and impairs cellular fitness, while chaperone levels and PC govern mutation rates via MMR saturation. A coupled feedback between protein synthesis quality and DNA replication fidelity can generate bistability, explaining sharp mutation-rate transitions and their reversibility with proteostasis interventions.

Mutation-rate plasticity and mutator dyn.hypothesis: Proteome damage during interspecies conjugation functions as a ‘compatibility gate’ by transiently downmodulating MMR, thereby enabling homeologous recombination proportional to donor–recipient divergence; antioxidant or chaperone interventions close this gate.
Mutation-rate plasticity and mutator dyn.research_question: In conjugations across increasing sequence divergence, do antioxidants (e.g., trolox) or chaperone overexpression reduce SOS induction and hybrid recombinant yield by preserving MMR activity, while experimentally elevating PC increases homeologous recombination even with intact MMR genes?
Mutation-rate plasticity and mutator dyn.rationale: SOS is induced during interspecies conjugation in proportion to divergence, and MMR blocks homeologous recombination but is readily saturated or downregulated under proteotoxic stress. If PC compromises MMR during conjugation, it would open a time-limited window for genome mixing; restoring proteostasis should reinstate the barrier.

Mutation-rate plasticity and mutator dyn.hypothesis: Cellular parabiosis non-cell-autonomously suppresses mutation rates by exporting DNA-repair capacity and redox buffering to neighboring cells; disruption of parabiosis by SASP-driven MMP activity or promotion agents acutely elevates local proteome oxidation and downregulates MRS activity, creating a transient mutator state that accelerates oncogenic initiation.
Mutation-rate plasticity and mutator dyn.research_question: In dense co-culture microtissues, does pharmacologic disruption of gap junctions or transient MMP activation increase spontaneous mutation rates in stressed cells, and is this prevented by antioxidants or exogenous complementation of MutS/MutH?
Mutation-rate plasticity and mutator dyn.rationale: Parabiosis phenotypically suppresses recessive defects via gap junctions and organelle transfer, while protein oxidation is the principal driver of spontaneous mutation. Inflammation/SASP and TPA-like promotion disrupt intercellular exchange, suggesting a non-cell-autonomous switch to a mutator state via increased proteome damage and functional MRS suppression.

Mutation-rate plasticity and mutator dyn.hypothesis: Age- or stress-induced decline in HSP90-mediated buffering converts accumulated mildly destabilizing polymorphisms into a proteome-oxidation feedback that triggers an SOS/MAC-like mutator switch via MRS depletion, producing a late-life 'mutational ignition' that precipitates cancer onset.
Mutation-rate plasticity and mutator dyn.research_question: Does partial inhibition of HSP90 in aged cells increase proteome carbonylation and spontaneous mutation rates through SOS induction and MRS depletion, and can antioxidants or restoring chaperone capacity prevent this switch?
Mutation-rate plasticity and mutator dyn.rationale: Chaperones buffer destabilizing mutations for decades, but when capacity wanes, protein misfolding and oxidation rise and are known to boost mutation rates. Concurrent SOS induction and stationary-phase MRS downregulation provide a mechanistic path to a late-onset mutator phenotype consistent with long disease latency.

Mutation-rate plasticity and mutator dyn.hypothesis: Translation-rate control via TOR signaling constitutes an antimutator axis: slowing translation reduces translational errors and proteome carbonylation, thereby lowering spontaneous DNA mutation rates independently of canonical DNA repair.
Mutation-rate plasticity and mutator dyn.research_question: Do TOR inhibitors (e.g., rapamycin) reduce proteome carbonylation and spontaneous mutation rates in bacteria and mammalian cells without altering MRS expression, and is the effect proportional to measured changes in translational error rates and speed?
Mutation-rate plasticity and mutator dyn.rationale: Protein oxidative damage drives spontaneous mutation rates. TOR-regulated translation speed affects translational error rates and likely proteome damage load; across species, longevity correlates with reduced translational errors and metabolism, implying a tunable, proteome-first route to lower mutagenesis.

Mutation-rate plasticity and mutator dyn.hypothesis: SOS-driven relaxation of mismatch repair during interspecies conjugation creates a transient high-recombination/high-mutation state that promotes hitchhiking and fixation of mutator alleles with acquired adaptive loci, explaining elevated mutator frequencies in HGT-adapting clinical pathogens.
Mutation-rate plasticity and mutator dyn.research_question: After Salmonella-to-E. coli conjugation, do SOS-induced recipient subpopulations show increased mutator allele frequencies and accelerated adaptation relative to intraspecies matings, and is this blocked by LexA(Ind−) or pharmacologic SOS inhibition?
Mutation-rate plasticity and mutator dyn.rationale: Interspecies conjugation strongly induces SOS, which alleviates genetic barriers via reduced MRS editing and increases recombination. Mutators hitchhike with adaptive changes; if HGT is enhanced under SOS, mutator alleles should be co-selected in recipient populations.

Mutation-rate plasticity and mutator dyn.hypothesis: A controlled 'promotion pulse' can be used diagnostically: brief, TIMP-buffered activation of MMPs or TPA-like agents transiently disrupts cellular parabiosis to unmask recessive mutations in dense tissues, enabling time-limited phenotypic readout of cryptic mutant burden without sustained inflammation.
Mutation-rate plasticity and mutator dyn.research_question: In high-density organoid cultures, do short MMP-activating or TPA pulses increase the detectable frequency of recessive drug-resistance phenotypes, and does co-administration of TIMPs confine the effect to a reversible diagnostic window?
Mutation-rate plasticity and mutator dyn.rationale: Promotion agents like TPA rapidly reveal recessive mutations at high density by interrupting phenotypic suppression via cellular parabiosis; protease activity is naturally limited by TIMPs and can be pulsed, suggesting a safe, transient method to expose hidden heterogeneity.

Mutation-rate plasticity and mutator dyn.hypothesis: Dietary modulation of the σS–MAC axis in the gut microbiome determines emergence of mutators and HGT: high-fiber, low-stress diets preserve MRS expression during stationary phase, reduce MAC mutagenesis, and curtail conjugational recombination, thereby suppressing fixation of mutator alleles in commensals and pathogens.
Mutation-rate plasticity and mutator dyn.research_question: Do dietary interventions that reduce stationary-phase stress (e.g., increased fermentable fiber) maintain MutS/MutH levels and lower MAC mutagenesis and conjugational recombination in gut E. coli, reducing mutator allele enrichment in vivo?
Mutation-rate plasticity and mutator dyn.rationale: Host diet shapes microbial adaptive mutation capacity. During stationary phase, σS-dependent programs downregulate MRS and elevate MAC and recombination, facilitating diversification and HGT; stabilizing physiology via diet should dampen this mutator-prone regime.

Restriction–modification systems.hypothesis: Bacteria transiently create spatially localized 'R–M safe harbors' at conjugation junctions by SOS-triggered inhibition of restriction endonucleases and double-strand exonucleases, combined with caging of incoming DNA in Dps-like condensates; this microdomain temporarily suppresses restriction and MMR editing to permit integration of foreign DNA delivered by type IV secretion as ssDNA.
Restriction–modification systems.research_question: Do SOS activation and conjugation jointly establish a spatial microdomain at the mating junction where restriction and exonuclease activities are locally inhibited and Dps-like condensates shield incoming DNA, thereby increasing horizontal gene acquisition while leaving genome-wide defense intact?
Restriction–modification systems.rationale: SOS alleviates restriction and inhibits ExoV to protect incoming DNA, and conjugative transfer often delivers ssDNA that is intrinsically less sensitive to restriction; Dps-driven DNA condensation can restrict diffusion and act as a molecular cage. A localized 'safe harbor' would reconcile strong global restriction with efficient HGT by confining antirestriction to the conjugation portal.

Restriction–modification systems.hypothesis: Restriction–modification loci are phase-variable mutator switches: stress and carbon-source starvation promote reversible frameshifts within microsatellite-like tracts in R–M promoters/coding sequences, toggling restriction/methylase stoichiometry and transiently lowering barrier functions to favor HGT and MAC, followed by reversion to a high-restriction, low-mutation state.
Restriction–modification systems.research_question: Do microsatellite-like sequences embedded in R–M genes or their regulators undergo stress- and starvation-enhanced slippage that phase-variably modulates restriction intensity and methylase levels, coupling bursts of horizontal acquisition and mutagenesis (MAC) to environmental conditions?
Restriction–modification systems.rationale: Bacteria install microsatellite-like tracts to render genes hypermutable, MAC is heightened under carbon-source starvation and varies among isolates, and selection can favor increased mutation rates when adaptation is mutation-limited. Variable R–M specificity is advantageous where diversity is selected, suggesting engineered phase variation within R–M modules could serve as an adaptive gate.

Restriction–modification systems.hypothesis: Conjugative plasmids export their own DNA methyltransferases (or specificity subunits) through the type IV secretion machinery into recipient cells prior to or during DNA transfer, pre-methylating the incoming DNA to match recipient R–M patterns and thereby achieving an 'epigenetic escort' that neutralizes restriction.
Restriction–modification systems.research_question: Can donor cells deliver active methyltransferases or specificity components into recipients via conjugation machinery to methylate transferred DNA in situ, and does this improve transfer across otherwise restrictive R–M barriers?
Restriction–modification systems.rationale: Conjugation is unusually immune to host restriction, prolonged mating saturates restriction, and phages commonly evade restriction by modifying their DNA; by analogy, T4SS-mediated protein transfer could pre-arm incoming DNA with protective methylation, explaining efficient spread of promiscuous plasmids across diverse hosts.

Restriction–modification systems.hypothesis: Mismatch-tolerant restriction endonucleases act as recombination editors by cleaving near-cognate recognition sites within heteroduplex DNA formed between divergent sequences, thereby partnering with MMR to enforce sequence-divergence-dependent barriers and drive speciation in sympatry.
Restriction–modification systems.research_question: Do restriction enzymes that tolerate single-base mismatches preferentially cut heteroduplex recombination intermediates at near-cognate sites when donor and recipient sequences diverge, reducing successful recombination in a divergence-dependent manner and synergizing with MMR to impose genetic isolation?
Restriction–modification systems.rationale: Many restriction enzymes tolerate single mismatches, while recombination barriers derive from both sequence divergence and MMR editing; a mismatch-tolerant REase could recognize and cleave heteroduplex DNA in divergent exchanges, providing an active, sequence-dependent enforcement layer that complements MMR.

Restriction–modification systems.hypothesis: Biofilm communities generate a 'communal methylome' by intercellular protein transfer through conjugative bridges and nanotube-like conduits, sharing methyltransferases to harmonize DNA modification states across strains; this reduces restriction of shared plasmids while preserving defense against unmodified phages.
Restriction–modification systems.research_question: Do bacteria in structured communities exchange active DNA methyltransferases between cells to synchronize methylation patterns, and does this coordinated methylome increase plasmid dissemination without compromising defense against phages lacking the community methylation signature?
Restriction–modification systems.rationale: Dozens of protein species can pass directly between cells through intercellular conduits, bacterial gene flow is highly promiscuous in structured environments, and certain 'amplifier' strains accelerate plasmid spread; exchanging methyltransferases could be an exapted mechanism enabling herd-level modulation of R–M barriers.

Restriction–modification systems.hypothesis: Under SOS/stress, bacteria redirect DNA methyltransferase activity to hypermethylate GATC motifs within contingency gene clusters, abolishing local strand discrimination by long-patch mismatch repair (LPMR) and thereby creating a spatially confined hypermutable state that accelerates adaptation while the rest of the genome remains repair-proficient.
Restriction–modification systems.research_question: Do stressed bacteria actively target Dam or orphan methyltransferases to contingency loci to increase local GATC methylation, suppress LPMR specifically at these loci, and thereby elevate mutation rates in contingency genes without raising genome-wide mutagenesis?
Restriction–modification systems.rationale: LPMR uses hemimethylated GATC to direct MutH-dependent repair; hypermethylation at both strands would block strand discrimination and allow replication errors and slippage mutations to persist. Bacteria already tune MR and SOS systemically and can target mutagenesis to contingency genes; inducible evolution suggests regulated locus-specific mechanisms could exist.

Restriction–modification systems.hypothesis: Bacteria execute time-bounded 'speciation pulses' by synchronizing transient suppression of restriction endonucleases with relaxation of mismatch repair strand discrimination via Dam modulation, permitting horizontal acquisition of partially homologous DNA during stress, followed by rapid reactivation of restriction–modification and LPMR to lock in new gene combinations and re-establish genetic isolation.
Restriction–modification systems.research_question: Can coordinated downregulation of restriction activity and modulation/inhibition of Dam-directed LPMR during stress increase acceptance of diverged DNA (facilitating HGT), with subsequent restoration of R–M and MMR creating a post-acquisition genetic firewall that drives punctuated speciation?
Restriction–modification systems.rationale: Inhibiting LPMR enables recombination with partially homologous sequences; SOS-driven MR downregulation and mutator selection occur during stress, while R–M systems define self versus non-self. Re-activation of MR and R–M after adaptation would restore isolation, reconciling vertical diversification with horizontal mosaics.

Restriction–modification systems.hypothesis: Temperate phages encode and deploy adenine methyltransferases during lysogeny to hypermethylate host GATC motifs genome-wide, neutralizing MutH-dependent strand discrimination and inducing a controlled mutator state that accelerates host adaptation to niches favorable for phage propagation; upon induction/excision, methyltransferase activity ceases and normal mismatch repair is restored.
Restriction–modification systems.research_question: Do prophage-encoded methyltransferases globally increase GATC methylation to suppress host LPMR, thereby elevating host mutation rates during lysogeny in a way that benefits phage ecology and fitness?
Restriction–modification systems.rationale: LPMR relies on Dam-mediated hemimethylation at GATC for strand discrimination; broad hypermethylation would impair correction, increasing mutation rates. Phage fitness is linked to GATC methylation state and hosts benefit from stress-induced mutator phases; selecting mechanisms that promote adaptation may be favored by phages.

DNA adducts and chemical carcinogenesis.hypothesis: Carcinogen-induced chromosomal rearrangements arise primarily from oxidative carbonylation of cohesin/condensin and fork-protection proteins, which weakens sister chromatid cohesion and biases double-strand break repair toward error-prone pathways, thereby increasing SCE and mis-joining independent of DNA adduct load.
DNA adducts and chemical carcinogenesis.research_question: Does selective protein carbonylation of cohesin/condensin and fork-protection complexes increase chromosomal rearrangements without changing DNA lesion burden, and can carbonyl scavengers or proteostasis enhancers suppress SCE and rearrangements under constant DNA damage?
DNA adducts and chemical carcinogenesis.rationale: Chromosomal rearrangements correlate more strongly with carcinogenicity than point mutations, and promoters like TPA increase SCE without detectable DNA damage. Protein carbonylation governs mutation rates by impairing DNA repair; carbonylation of cohesion/repair machinery would directly shift recombination and repair outcomes toward rearrangements.

DNA adducts and chemical carcinogenesis.hypothesis: Inducible mutagenesis is amplified by DNA damage-triggered activation of trypsin-like proteases that selectively cleave oxidatively carbonylated replication and repair proteins, converting repairable DNA lesions into fixed mutations; thus, protease inhibitors preserve repair capacity and blunt mutagenesis and promotion.
DNA adducts and chemical carcinogenesis.research_question: Do DNA-damaging agents and tumor promoters increase specific protease activity toward carbonylated DNA maintenance proteins, and do broad-spectrum or targeted trypsin-like protease inhibitors reduce mutation fixation and tumor promotion at unchanged DNA adduct levels?
DNA adducts and chemical carcinogenesis.rationale: DNA damage induces proteases (e.g., plasminogen activator), and protease inhibitors suppress both tumorigenesis and UV mutagenesis. Since carbonylated proteins are preferentially degraded and protein carbonylation dictates mutation rates by limiting repair, protease activation would further deplete repair capacity and fix mutations.

DNA adducts and chemical carcinogenesis.hypothesis: The mutagenic efficiency of a given DNA adduct is governed by its residence time at stalled replication forks, which creates local ‘carbonylation microdomains’ that oxidatively disable mismatch repair and base-excision repair proteins in cis, increasing residual lesions and mutation fixation despite identical adduct numbers.
DNA adducts and chemical carcinogenesis.research_question: Does prolonging fork–adduct engagement increase localized protein carbonylation and suppress nearby repair, thereby boosting mutations per adduct, and can interventions that reduce fork stalling (or locally scavenge carbonyls) lower mutagenicity at constant adduct burden?
DNA adducts and chemical carcinogenesis.rationale: Induced mutation frequencies correlate with residual, unrepaired DNA damage and with total proteome carbonylation, not with initial DNA damage. A mechanistic link is that prolonged adduct–fork interactions generate localized oxidative stress that carbonylates nearby repair proteins, reducing repair and increasing fixation.

DNA adducts and chemical carcinogenesis.hypothesis: Chronic sterile inflammation functions as a ‘proteome mutagen’ in the two-stage model by elevating carbonylation specifically in the DNA maintenance proteome within initiated clones, thereby converting sub-mutagenic initiator exposures into highly mutagenic regimes that fix residual adducts into mutations.
DNA adducts and chemical carcinogenesis.research_question: In initiated tissues, does prolonged promoter-driven inflammation increase carbonylation of replication/repair proteins and residual DNA damage, and can targeted anti-carbonyl or proteostasis therapies during the promotion phase reduce mutation fixation and tumor yield?
DNA adducts and chemical carcinogenesis.rationale: Promotion by TPA accelerates tumor emergence without direct DNA damage and can increase SCE and transiently inhibit replication. Inflammation and ECM remodeling generate radicals, and protein carbonylation dictates mutation rates and repair bottlenecks, providing a direct route by which inflammation amplifies initiator-induced mutagenesis.

DNA adducts and chemical carcinogenesis.hypothesis: Carbonylation-driven aggregation of replication fidelity subunits (e.g., proofreading exonucleases and mismatch repair proteins) seeds heritable ‘proteotoxic mutator’ states that persist across mitoses independent of DNA sequence change, creating clonal fields predisposed to carcinogenesis.
DNA adducts and chemical carcinogenesis.research_question: Do carbonylated aggregates of DNA fidelity proteins persist and propagate through cell divisions to confer stable mutator phenotypes, and can chaperone enhancement or disaggregation reverse these proteotoxic mutator states and lower cancer initiation?
DNA adducts and chemical carcinogenesis.rationale: Carbonylation precedes and promotes aggregation, which can become proteolysis-resistant; GroEL upregulation tracks protein carbonylation, and mutation rates scale steeply with protein carbonylation. Oxidative damage to the DNA maintenance proteome limits fidelity, suggesting aggregated fidelity factors could encode heritable mutator epimutations.

DNA adducts and chemical carcinogenesis.hypothesis: Carbonyl-affinity nanoconjugates that localize to replication factories and scavenge protein carbonyls will reduce mutation rates far more effectively than bulk antioxidants by preventing ‘repair bottleneck’ carbonylation of the DNA maintenance proteome in situ.
DNA adducts and chemical carcinogenesis.research_question: Can aminooxy-functional nanoconjugates, optionally GSH-loaded, targeted to replisome markers or carbonylated proteins at forks, decrease local protein carbonylation and mutation frequencies without altering initial DNA adduct levels in cells and tissues?
DNA adducts and chemical carcinogenesis.rationale: Reducing proteome carbonylation at constant ROS lowers mutation rates by an order of magnitude, and mutation frequencies track proteome carbonylation rather than initial DNA damage. Aminooxy nanoconjugates form stable oximes with carbonyls and show enhanced protection in the presence of glutathione, making them suitable localized countermeasures.

DNA adducts and chemical carcinogenesis.hypothesis: Bulky miscoding DNA adducts nucleate localized 'oxidative repair zones' in which stalled replisomes/topoisomerases generate ROS that carbonylate nearby repair and recombination proteins, biasing double-strand break processing toward error-prone recombination and thus promoting chromosomal rearrangements as a rate-limiting step in carcinogenesis.
DNA adducts and chemical carcinogenesis.research_question: Do persistent bulky DNA adducts increase localized ROS and protein carbonylation at damage foci, causing oxidation of recombination/repair factors and a shift from high-fidelity repair to rearrangement-prone pathways?
DNA adducts and chemical carcinogenesis.rationale: DNA-damaging agents generate ROS that oxidize proteins; protein carbonylation correlates strongly with lethality and mutagenesis and can render repair activities error-prone. Carcinogens also stimulate recombination and chromosomal rearrangements. Quinolone-induced topoisomerase perturbation increases protein carbonylation, suggesting that DNA processing stress can locally drive proteome oxidation and pathway choice.

DNA adducts and chemical carcinogenesis.hypothesis: Persistent εA/εC etheno DNA adducts produced by vinyl chloride/CEO saturate MutS/MutL mismatch repair in vivo, mimicking retron-induced MutS titration, thereby elevating homologous and non-allelic recombination and precipitating chromosomal rearrangements that drive carcinogenic initiation.
DNA adducts and chemical carcinogenesis.research_question: Does increasing εA/εC adduct burden proportionally deplete functional MMR capacity and elevate recombination and chromosomal rearrangement frequencies in exposed cells?
DNA adducts and chemical carcinogenesis.rationale: εA/εC are miscoding, persistent adducts formed by vinyl chloride metabolites. MMR saturation/titration by mismatches increases mutagenesis and interspecies recombination. Given the tight link between recombination, rearrangements, and carcinogenesis, MMR sequestration by etheno adducts could mechanistically connect vinyl chloride exposure to rearrangement-centric initiation.

DNA adducts and chemical carcinogenesis.hypothesis: Oxidative carbonylation of the replicative polymerase holoenzyme (Pol III in bacteria; Pol δ/ε and PCNA in eukaryotes) enforces a constitutive switch to error-prone translesion polymerases, converting non-mutagenic promoters and modest oxidative stressors into highly mutagenic episodes in initiated cells.
DNA adducts and chemical carcinogenesis.research_question: Does ROS-driven carbonylation of core replisome components increase TLS engagement and mutation load independent of DNA lesion burden, thereby explaining promotion by non-mutagenic agents?
DNA adducts and chemical carcinogenesis.rationale: Modification of Pol III can enable constitutive UV mutagenesis, and XP-V phenotypes show that TLS choice dictates mutational outcomes. Protein carbonylation is more tightly linked to mutagenesis than canonical DNA oxidation markers, and oxidation of repair proteins yields error-prone activities. Thus, promoter-induced ROS may drive a polymerase switch mechanistically underpinning promotion.

DNA adducts and chemical carcinogenesis.hypothesis: Nuclear delivery of Deinococcus radiodurans-like manganese–metabolite antioxidant complexes selectively protects recombination and repair proteins from ROS-induced carbonylation during genotoxic exposure, thereby suppressing carcinogen-induced chromosomal rearrangements and initiation without altering DNA adduct formation.
DNA adducts and chemical carcinogenesis.research_question: Can targeted Mn–metabolite complexes reproduce Deinococcus’s low-protein-oxidation state in mammalian nuclei and reduce rearrangement frequencies under carcinogen exposure while leaving DNA lesion spectra unchanged?
DNA adducts and chemical carcinogenesis.rationale: D. radiodurans accumulates Mn–metabolite complexes that protect proteins but not DNA and exhibits low protein carbonylation with extreme stress resistance. Since protein carbonylation tracks mutagenesis and rearrangement-linked carcinogenesis, shielding protein machineries during DNA damage could decouple DNA lesions from downstream oncogenic rearrangements.

Bacterial mutagenicity assays.hypothesis: In naturally competent bacteria, RecA filaments assembled on imported ssDNA nucleate localized LexA cleavage and recruitment of translesion polymerases (Pol IV/V), creating a transient hypermutagenic zone within ~5–20 kb of the recombination site that accelerates compatibility mutations enabling stable integration and expression of horizontally acquired genes.
Bacterial mutagenicity assays.research_question: During natural transformation, do mutation rates and spectra increase specifically within kilobase-scale windows around integration tracts in a RecA-, dinB-, and umuDC-dependent manner without a corresponding genome-wide increase?
Bacterial mutagenicity assays.rationale: SOS is triggered in competent cells even without exogenous DNA damage, and SOS upregulates recombination and error-prone polymerases. Coupling RecA activation on incoming DNA to local TLS recruitment would focus mutations near recombination breakpoints, reconciling stress-induced mutagenesis with efficient horizontal gene assimilation.

Bacterial mutagenicity assays.hypothesis: Translation of SOS TLS polymerases (dinB/umuDC) is gated by metabolite- and metal-sensitive rare codon clusters that act as conditional ‘mutator throttles’; under metabolic stress (e.g., cAMP regulon activation) and elevated intracellular Mn2+, ribosome pausing lifts translational repression to produce a sharp, switch-like increase in Pol IV/V abundance and activity.
Bacterial mutagenicity assays.research_question: Does synonymous recoding of dinB and umuDC to high-CAI codons flatten stress- and Mn2+-dependent increases in mutagenesis, and can Mn2+ chelation or codon-cluster mutagenesis modulate TLS protein levels and mutation spectra during SOS?
Bacterial mutagenicity assays.rationale: TLS polymerase genes are not highly expressed and show codon usage comparable to average genes, and SOS-driven adaptive mutagenesis is tied to metabolic stress. Mn2+ is mutagenic in vitro; a translational gate integrating metabolic and metal cues would provide rapid, resource-efficient control over mutator capacity.

Bacterial mutagenicity assays.hypothesis: Genomes of damaged bacteriophages act as ‘mutagenic sponges’ that titrate host DNA repair and activate RecA-dependent SOS, thereby elevating host genomic mutagenesis even without direct host DNA damage; the effect scales with the phage DNA damage load and repair capacity.
Bacterial mutagenicity assays.research_question: Does infection with UV- or gamma-damaged λ phage increase host mutation rates in a RecA-dependent manner by sequestering repair proteins, and can repair-protein recruitment to phage DNA be quantitatively linked to elevated host mutation burden?
Bacterial mutagenicity assays.rationale: Irradiated phage increase mutant yields even in unirradiated hosts and the SOS system underlies mutagenic responses. A mechanistic model where damaged phage DNA consumes repair capacity and triggers SOS explains indirect mutagenesis and predicts virome-dependent evolvability.

Bacterial mutagenicity assays.hypothesis: Under SOS-inducing stress, E. coli partitions mutagenic activity to transposable-element neighborhoods by preferential recruitment of Pol IV/V to transposon excision/repair intermediates, promoting local deletions and rearrangements (e.g., cryptic operon eliminations) while Pol II exerts antimutagenic control at replication forks to limit genome-wide base substitutions.
Bacterial mutagenicity assays.research_question: Are mutation and structural-variant densities enriched within ±5 kb of IS elements during starvation-induced SOS, and is this enrichment dependent on dinB, umuC, recA, and ruv genes while overall base-substitution rates remain constrained by polB?
Bacterial mutagenicity assays.rationale: Transposon excision increases in mutator backgrounds, SOS orchestrates recombination and TLS polymerases that can be mutagenic or antimutagenic depending on context, and deletions of cryptic operons are frequent in natural isolates. A ‘damage partitioning’ mechanism would concentrate risky mutations where genome plasticity is tolerated.

Bacterial mutagenicity assays.hypothesis: Horizontal acquisition of adhesin/pili operons is frequently accompanied by linked mutator determinants (e.g., MMR modulators or TLS regulators) on the same genomic islands, enabling a transient, SOS-repressible hypermutable phase that accelerates host-range adaptation before LexA-mediated repression restores low mutation rates.
Bacterial mutagenicity assays.research_question: Do recent acquisitions of pap/prs-like operons co-occur with mutator phenotypes or polymorphisms in mismatch repair/TLS regulation in natural isolates more often than expected by chance, and does this association decay over evolutionary time?
Bacterial mutagenicity assays.rationale: Key virulence operons are horizontally transferred, natural populations harbor mutators at higher-than-expected frequencies, and mutators provide short-term adaptive benefits before being selected against once adapted. Genomic linkage of virulence and mutability could be an evolvability strategy.

Bacterial mutagenicity assays.hypothesis: Lesion-specific recruitment of TLS polymerases determines the divergent carcinogenicity of vinyl chloride metabolites: CEO-induced etheno adducts preferentially recruit Pol IV, producing clustered base-substitution mutagenesis, whereas CAA adducts preferentially engage Pol II for largely error-free bypass; the differential dynamics can be resolved in live cells by exploiting the intrinsic fluorescence of etheno adducts.
Bacterial mutagenicity assays.research_question: Do fluorescent etheno-adduct foci formed by CEO versus CAA show distinct colocalization with Pol IV versus Pol II in live cells, and do polB or dinB deletions swap the mutation spectra and reduce CEO-specific mutagenic clustering?
Bacterial mutagenicity assays.rationale: VC metabolites produce etheno adducts with characteristic fluorescence; CEO is tumorigenic while CAA is not. TLS polymerases can be mutagenic or antimutagenic depending on lesion context, suggesting lesion-selective polymerase engagement underlies the risk differential and can be visualized to build mechanism-based mutagenicity assays.

Bacterial mutagenicity assays.hypothesis: Proteome carbonylation is an upstream master switch that gates sigmaS-dependent MAC and conjugation-triggered SOS; pharmacologic carbonyl scavengers or proteostasis boosters administered during antibiotic treatment will stabilize mismatch repair (MutS/MutL), suppress stress-induced mutagenesis and interspecies horizontal gene transfer, and thereby markedly reduce the emergence of antibiotic resistance without compromising bactericidal efficacy.
Bacterial mutagenicity assays.research_question: Do carbonyl-scavenging or proteostasis-enhancing adjuvants reduce sigmaS-dependent MAC and conjugation-induced SOS by preserving MutS/MutL levels and function, thereby lowering both mutation supply and HGT under antibiotic stress?
Bacterial mutagenicity assays.rationale: Protein oxidation elevates spontaneous mutation rates and is required for MAC, while stationary-phase and strain-specific depletion of MutS promotes stress mutagenesis. Interspecies conjugation potently induces SOS, aiding recombination and mutagenesis. By limiting protein carbonylation, MutS stability and repair capacity should be maintained, blunting both MAC and conjugation-driven SOS, thus curbing adaptive evolution during therapy.

Bacterial mutagenicity assays.hypothesis: Non-genotoxic 'promotion-like' agents can increase bacterial mutant yield by enhancing recombination-mediated unmasking and fixation of pre-existing variants without increasing de novo mutation rates; a bacterial mutagenicity assay that adds a controlled 'promotion module' (e.g., transient RecA/RuvAB upregulation during high-density or aging-colony growth) will reveal promoter activity analogous to mammalian tumor promotion and improve hazard prediction.
Bacterial mutagenicity assays.research_question: Can a two-stage bacterial assay that separates initiation (mutagenesis) from promotion (recombination/segregation and expression) detect non-mutagenic promoters by elevating mutant expression at constant mutation input?
Bacterial mutagenicity assays.rationale: In mammals, TPA-like promoters are nonmutagenic yet increase SCE and accelerate tumor emergence and resistance expression. In bacteria, SOS upregulates recombination genes, and combined M×R indices predict carcinogenic potency. Introducing a controlled recombination/segregation 'promotion' phase should analogously amplify phenotypic expression of existing variants, distinguishing promoters from initiators.

Bacterial mutagenicity assays.hypothesis: Under oxidative stress, localized translational infidelity at regulatory leader/triplet-repeat elements linked to bacterial contingency genes produces trans-acting factors that transiently sequester the limited MutS/MutL pool away from those loci, creating neighborhood-specific MMR depletion and a targeted mutational burst confined to contingency genes.
Bacterial mutagenicity assays.research_question: Does oxidative protein damage induce locus-specific translational errors that reallocate scarce MMR components, increasing local mutation rates at contingency genes relative to the genomic background?
Bacterial mutagenicity assays.rationale: Contingency genes are preferentially diversified under selection, MutS/MutL copy numbers are low, and protein oxidation elevates mutation rates. Although baseline misreading is rare, stress-activated sigmaS programs and proteome oxidation could bias translation of specific leaders, transiently altering MMR localization and producing targeted hypermutation without a global fidelity collapse.

Bacterial mutagenicity assays.hypothesis: A synthetic MutS-stabilizing circuit (constitutive, RpoS-insensitive mutS expression combined with carbonylation-resistant MutS variants) will selectively suppress sigmaS-driven stress mutagenesis and sequence-divergent (homeologous) recombination, while leaving homologous recombination intact, thereby decoupling essential repair from adaptive evolution and sharply limiting resistance evolution during gut colonization and in aging colonies.
Bacterial mutagenicity assays.research_question: Can engineered stabilization of MMR specifically reduce stress-induced mutation and homeologous recombination without impairing homologous recombination and viability, and does this curtail adaptive evolution in vivo?
Bacterial mutagenicity assays.rationale: MMR limits both spontaneous mutations and homeologous recombination, and its downregulation during stationary phase is sigmaS-linked. MutS defects massively elevate interspecies recombination, facilitating mosaicism and adaptation. Stabilizing MutS through expression control and oxidation resistance should prevent the stress 'learning window,' reducing both mutation supply and recombination across sequence divergence while preserving normal homologous recombination.

Bacterial mutagenicity assays.hypothesis: Protein carbonylation functions as an oxidation-gated mutator switch in bacteria: when proteome carbonylation exceeds a threshold, oxidation-driven destabilization of MutS/MutL and activation of RecA/SOS transiently suppresses mismatch repair and elevates error-prone replication, thereby increasing genome-wide mutation rates; boosting manganese-mediated antioxidant influx (via OxyR) or adding Deinococcus-derived antioxidant complexes will raise the threshold and suppress the mutator switch.
Bacterial mutagenicity assays.research_question: Does experimentally increasing proteome carbonylation in E. coli trigger a coordinated drop in MutS/MutL abundance or activity and a rise in SOS-dependent mutagenesis, and can manganese supplementation or Deinococcus protein-free extracts prevent this transition and reduce mutation rates without impairing viability?
Bacterial mutagenicity assays.rationale: Proteome carbonylation tightly correlates with bacterial killing and has been proposed as a primary cause of radiosensitivity; E. coli downregulates MutS in stationary phase when stress-induced mutagenesis emerges, and aging colonies show SOS and mutagenesis without exogenous DNA damage. The OxyR response drives manganese import, and Deinococcus-derived antioxidant systems protect proteins and cells; thus, oxidation likely tunes the balance between high-fidelity repair and inducible mutator pathways.

Bacterial mutagenicity assays.hypothesis: Nonenzymatic manganese–small-molecule complexes and a heightened pentose phosphate pathway form an 'antimutagenic sink' in Deinococcus that scavenges oxidized dNTPs and protects replisome proteins, thereby suppressing translesion synthesis and SOS mutagenesis while maintaining viability; engineering this manganese–metabolite buffering network into E. coli will create radiation-hardened, low-mutator strains.
Bacterial mutagenicity assays.research_question: Do Deinococcus-like manganese complexes and elevated PPP flux in E. coli reduce intracellular 8-oxo-dNTP pools and stabilize replication proteins to lower SOS/TLS-dependent mutagenesis under radiation or oxidative stress without decreasing survival, and can this be recapitulated by expressing Deinococcus antioxidative systems or supplementing defined Mn–metabolite complexes?
Bacterial mutagenicity assays.rationale: Radiation lethality tracks protein oxidation across species, and Deinococcus resists it via high Mn/Fe ratios, strong ROS scavenging by protein-free extracts, and elevated PPP; MutT-like systems detoxify oxidized nucleotides. Together, these features plausibly divert oxidized metabolites and protect polymerase III/protein targets, reducing reliance on error-prone bypass.

Bacterial mutagenicity assays.hypothesis: Metabolic activation systems (S9 mix) potentiate epigenetically controlled mutagenic machinery in bacteria by generating reactive metabolites that preferentially induce proteome carbonylation and saturate mismatch repair, shifting outcomes from gene-specific point mutations toward genome-wide epigenetic switching; this explains enhanced epigenetic responses (e.g., to aflatoxin B1) and predicts compound-specific 'epigenetic-to-mutagenic' fingerprints.
Bacterial mutagenicity assays.research_question: Do S9-activated metabolites increase proteome carbonylation and MMR saturation in E. coli, thereby boosting epigenetic reporter switching far above point mutation rates, and can manipulating MMR capacity (mutH/mutS backgrounds) or antioxidant buffering rebalance the epigenetic-to-mutagenic response ratio for specific carcinogens?
Bacterial mutagenicity assays.rationale: Epigenetic responses exceed mutagenic responses by orders of magnitude and are enhanced by S9 for aflatoxin B1; many indirect genetic effects arise from epigenetically controlled machinery. High lesion loads can saturate MMR, and protein oxidation is a dominant stress output; together, S9-driven metabolite chemistry likely tilts assays toward epigenetic switches rather than single-locus mutations.

Bacterial mutagenicity assays.hypothesis: In structured, oxygen-limited microenvironments (aging colonies/biofilms), microniche-specific proteome carbonylation gradients spatially disable mismatch repair at cell poles, generating localized MutL foci and mutation hotspots; enhancing manganese import (OxyR-dependent) or adding Deinococcus antioxidants will flatten these gradients and suppress spatially biased emergence of antibiotic resistance.
Bacterial mutagenicity assays.research_question: Do microfluidic oxygen gradients and colony-depth niches create spatial proteome carbonylation patterns that correlate with loss of MutS/MutL function and MutL-CFP mutation foci in E. coli, and can manganese supplementation or Deinococcus protein-free extracts homogenize PC levels and reduce localized adaptive mutagenesis in colonies and biofilms?
Bacterial mutagenicity assays.rationale: SOS and mutagenesis arise in aging colonies without exogenous DNA damage and structured environments shape bacterial fitness; proteome carbonylation tracks killing and stress, and OxyR drives manganese import. Real-time MutL-CFP imaging can reveal spatial mutation bursts that antioxidants might attenuate.
